title: Biological & Evolutionary Anthropology
subtitle: Human origins, fossil record & comparative primatology
methodology: METHODOLOGY · Every entry anchors to a landmark fossil discovery, genetic study, field observation or theoretical text. The hint explains the idea in plain language; the note names the primary publication and flags replication status, revisions and known controversies. Studies and effects carry a replicability badge — 🟢 confirmed to high confidence · 🟡 nuanced, contested or partially revised · 🔴 failed or severely disputed. Map pins mark the fossil site, field location or institution where the work was carried out.

categories.label: Theories & Models
categories.subtitle: The frameworks that organise how humans evolved, spread, and became who we are

entries.label: Out-of-Africa Replacement Model
entries.hint: Modern humans evolved recently in Africa (roughly 200,000 years ago) and then dispersed worldwide, replacing existing archaic populations like Neanderthals with little or no interbreeding. The model was proposed in direct opposition to the idea that regional populations evolved in parallel from earlier hominins already living across Eurasia.
entries.note: Stringer, C.B. & Andrews, P. (1988). 'Genetic and Fossil Evidence for the Origin of Modern Humans.' Science, 239(4845), 1263–1268. The strict 'little or no interbreeding' clause was substantially revised after Neanderthal and Denisovan genome sequencing (2010) confirmed low-level admixture (see ef4); the African-origin timing and dispersal framework itself remains the dominant model.

entries.label: Multiregional Continuity Model
entries.loc: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan
entries.hint: Rather than a single recent African replacement, modern humans arose through continuous evolution and gene flow between regional archaic populations across Africa, Europe, and Asia — meaning today's regional populations partly trace their ancestry to hominins that had lived in the same regions for over a million years.
entries.note: Wolpoff, M.H., Wu, X. & Thorne, A.G. (1984). 'Modern Homo sapiens Origins: A General Theory of Hominid Evolution Involving the Fossil Evidence.' In F.H. Smith & F. Spencer (eds.), The Origins of Modern Humans, Alan R. Liss. Genomic evidence has decisively favoured the Out-of-Africa model's core African-origin timing (see th1), though the small admixture fraction confirmed by ancient DNA gives the multiregional model's central claim of regional genetic continuity a modest degree of vindication.

entries.label: Savanna Hypothesis
entries.loc: University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, South Africa
entries.hint: Early hominins evolved upright walking as an adaptation to life on the open savanna after forests receded in East and southern Africa — freeing the hands, improving heat dissipation, and extending sightlines over tall grass. It was the dominant explanation for bipedal origins for most of the twentieth century.
entries.note: Dart, R.A. (1925). 'Australopithecus africanus: The Man-Ape of South Africa.' Nature, 115, 195–199, first framed the savanna setting as central to human origins. Palaeoenvironmental reconstruction of early Australopithecus and Ardipithecus sites (WoldeGabriel et al. 1994, Nature; White et al. 2009, Science) later showed several key hominin fossils come from wooded, not open grassland, habitats — badly undermining the hypothesis in its strict form (see st11).

entries.label: Endurance Running Hypothesis
entries.hint: The genus Homo evolved a distinctive suite of anatomical features — long legs, short toes, an enlarged gluteus maximus, an elastic Achilles tendon and nuchal ligament, and an efficient sweating system — specifically to run long distances, most plausibly to persistence-hunt game by chasing it to exhaustion in the midday heat before projectile weapons existed.
entries.note: Bramble, D.M. & Lieberman, D.E. (2004). 'Endurance Running and the Evolution of Homo.' Nature, 432, 345–352. Ethnographic persistence-hunting has been directly documented among the San of the Kalahari (Liebenberg 2006, Current Anthropology) as a plausible modern analogue, though it is now rare and its prevalence in deep prehistory cannot be directly tested.

entries.label: Provisioning Model of Bipedal Origins
entries.hint: Bipedalism evolved because it freed males' hands to carry food back to a home base for a monogamous mate and offspring, reducing male-male competition and increasing reproductive success — a social and reproductive explanation for bipedal origins rather than a purely locomotor or thermoregulatory one.
entries.note: Lovejoy, C.O. (1981). 'The Origin of Man.' Science, 211(4480), 341–350. Reduced canine size and body-size sexual dimorphism, both predicted by the model, are present in Ardipithecus ramidus (see st11), offering some support, but the monogamy assumption is difficult to test directly from skeletal or fossil evidence alone and remains contested.

entries.label: Social Brain Hypothesis
entries.hint: Primate brain size, and especially neocortex size relative to the rest of the brain, correlates with the typical size of a species' social group — proposed to reflect the cognitive demands of tracking relationships, alliances, and reputations within a complex social network, rather than the demands of tool use or foraging alone.
entries.note: Dunbar, R.I.M. (1992). 'Neocortex Size as a Constraint on Group Size in Primates.' Journal of Human Evolution, 22(6), 469–493. The extrapolated human figure — 'Dunbar's number' of roughly 150 stable social relationships — has drawn substantial criticism (Lindenfors et al. 2021, Biology Letters) for resting on a weak statistical relationship and inconsistent modern social-network data; the general brain-size/sociality correlation across primates is more robust than the specific human number.

entries.label: Grandmother Hypothesis
entries.loc: University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah
entries.hint: Human females' unusually long post-reproductive lifespan evolved because grandmothers who stopped reproducing themselves and instead helped provision and care for grandchildren increased their own genetic legacy more than continuing to bear children directly would have.
entries.note: Hawkes, K., O'Connell, J.F., Blurton Jones, N.G., Alvarez, H. & Charnov, E.L. (1998). 'Grandmothering, Menopause, and the Evolution of Human Life Histories.' Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 95(3), 1336–1339, based on Hadza foraging data from Tanzania. Comparative work on post-reproductive lifespans in orca and pilot whales (Croft et al. 2017, Current Biology) shows the same grandmother effect can evolve independently in non-primate, highly social mammals, strengthening the underlying logic.

entries.label: Expensive Tissue Hypothesis
entries.hint: The human brain is metabolically very costly to run, but humans do not have an unusually high overall metabolic rate for a primate of their body size — the hypothesis proposes that a shrinking, less costly gut, enabled by a higher-quality, more digestible diet, freed the metabolic budget that supported brain expansion.
entries.note: Aiello, L.C. & Wheeler, P. (1995). 'The Expensive-Tissue Hypothesis: The Brain and the Digestive System in Human and Primate Evolution.' Current Anthropology, 36(2), 199–221. Subsequent comparative analyses (Navarrete, van Schaik & Isler 2011, Nature) found the predicted gut-brain trade-off does not hold cleanly across all mammals, suggesting increased total energy intake, not gut reduction specifically, may be the more general explanation.

entries.label: Toba Catastrophe / Genetic Bottleneck Theory
entries.loc: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, Illinois
entries.hint: The eruption of the Toba supervolcano in Sumatra roughly 74,000 years ago is proposed to have triggered a severe, multi-year volcanic winter that crashed the human population to a few thousand breeding individuals, leaving a genetic bottleneck said to be visible in modern human DNA's relatively low diversity compared to other great apes.
entries.note: Ambrose, S.H. (1998). 'Late Pleistocene Human Population Bottlenecks, Volcanic Winter, and Differentiation of Modern Humans.' Journal of Human Evolution, 34(6), 623–651. The theory has been substantially undermined: archaeological sites in India (Petraglia et al. 2007, Science) show continuous human occupation across the Toba ash layer with no disruption, and genetic bottleneck estimates timed to 74,000 years ago have not held up under more recent, denser genomic sampling (Yost et al. 2018, Journal of Human Evolution). Widely cited as a cautionary example of an appealing but weakly supported catastrophist narrative.

entries.label: Dual Inheritance Theory
entries.loc: University of California, Los Angeles, California
entries.hint: Human evolution has run on two intertwined inheritance systems at once — genes and culturally transmitted information such as skills, norms, and technology — each shaping the selective pressures on the other; culturally acquired traits like dairying or cooking can create genuine genetic selection pressure, and genetic predispositions can bias what cultural traits spread.
entries.note: Boyd, R. & Richerson, P.J. (1985). Culture and the Evolutionary Process. University of Chicago Press. The dairying-and-lactase-persistence case (see ef1) is the most frequently cited real-world confirmation of gene-culture coevolution; critics (e.g. Lewens 2015, Cultural Evolution) argue the framework's mathematical models are harder to test rigorously outside such clean, single-gene cases.

categories.label: Landmark Studies
categories.subtitle: The defining experiments — and exactly what they found

entries.label: The Taung Child
entries.hint: A fossilised juvenile skull, found by lime-quarry workers and sent to anatomist Raymond Dart, combined an ape-sized brain with a forward-positioned foramen magnum — the hole where the spinal cord exits the skull — indicating the head balanced atop an upright spine rather than in front of it like a quadruped's. It was the first Australopithecus ever identified and the first strong fossil evidence that upright walking preceded large brain size in human evolution.
entries.note: Dart, R.A. (1925). 'Australopithecus africanus: The Man-Ape of South Africa.' Nature, 115, 195–199. Dart's claim was widely dismissed for two decades by a scientific establishment still committed to the fraudulent Piltdown Man's brain-first narrative (see db3); Robert Broom's subsequent adult Australopithecus finds at Sterkfontein in the 1930s–40s vindicated Dart's interpretation.

entries.label: Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis)
entries.hint: Donald Johanson and Tom Gray found roughly 40% of a single Australopithecus afarensis skeleton eroding out of a gully — an extraordinary completeness for a 3.2-million-year-old hominin. The pelvis and knee joint showed unambiguous adaptations for habitual bipedal walking, even though the skull retained an ape-sized brain, definitively separating the evolution of upright walking from the evolution of a large brain.
entries.note: Johanson, D.C. & Taieb, M. (1976). 'Plio-Pleistocene Hominid Discoveries in Hadar, Ethiopia.' Nature, 260, 293–297. Named 'Lucy' after the Beatles song 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds' played at the celebration camp that evening. Later finds of the same species, including the 'First Family' site (AL 333) and the juvenile 'Selam,' confirmed A. afarensis as a well-established, bipedal, small-brained hominin lineage.

entries.label: Laetoli Footprints
entries.hint: A trail of roughly 70 fossilised hominin footprints, preserved in volcanic ash and dated to 3.66 million years ago, shows a walking gait with a human-like heel-strike-to-toe-off pattern and a big toe aligned with the other toes rather than opposable like an ape's — direct physical evidence of habitual bipedal walking a full 1.5 million years before the genus Homo existed.
entries.note: Leakey, M.D. & Hay, R.L. (1979). 'Pliocene Footprints in the Laetolil Beds at Laetoli, Northern Tanzania.' Nature, 278, 317–323. Attributed most plausibly to Australopithecus afarensis, found nearby and dated to the same period (see st2). A long-running debate over whether the gait retained a more bent-hip, bent-knee ape-like component (Raichlen et al. 2010, PLOS ONE) rather than a fully modern one remains only partly resolved.

entries.label: Turkana Boy
entries.hint: Kamoya Kimeu, working with Richard Leakey's team, found the most complete early hominin skeleton ever recovered — a roughly 8-to-10-year-old Homo erectus boy who died 1.5 million years ago. His tall, narrow, long-limbed body plan closely resembles modern equatorial human proportions, showing that essentially modern human body proportions had evolved well before modern brain size or modern behaviour.
entries.note: Brown, F., Harris, J., Leakey, R. & Walker, A. (1985). 'Early Homo erectus Skeleton from West Lake Turkana, Kenya.' Nature, 316, 788–792. Estimates of his projected adult height (approximately 1.85 m) were later revised slightly downward (Graves et al. 2010, Journal of Human Evolution) once growth-curve assumptions for his age at death were reconsidered, but the core body-proportion finding stands.

entries.label: Homo naledi / Rising Star Cave
entries.loc: Rising Star Cave, Cradle of Humankind, South Africa
entries.hint: Cavers found a chamber accessible only through a near-vertical 12-metre chute containing the disarticulated remains of at least 15 individuals of a previously unknown small-brained hominin, Homo naledi, with a strange mosaic of primitive and modern anatomical traits. The remoteness and difficulty of the chamber's access led the discovery team to controversially propose deliberate body disposal by the naledi themselves.
entries.note: Berger, L.R. et al. (2015). 'Homo naledi, a New Species of the Genus Homo from the Dinaledi Chamber, South Africa.' eLife, 4, e09560. Uranium-thorium and other dating (Dirks et al. 2017, eLife) surprisingly placed the fossils at just 236,000–335,000 years old — far more recent than the primitive anatomy would suggest, meaning naledi overlapped in time with early Homo sapiens. The deliberate-disposal interpretation (see db8) remains actively disputed.

entries.label: Sahelanthropus tchadensis
entries.hint: A nearly complete cranium nicknamed 'Toumaï,' dated to roughly 7 million years old, is among the very oldest fossils ever proposed as a hominin — right around the molecular-clock estimate for the human-chimpanzee split. Its forward-positioned foramen magnum was cited as evidence of bipedalism, but no complete limb bones have been found, so its locomotion and even its status as a true hominin remain genuinely contested.
entries.note: Brunet, M. et al. (2002). 'A New Hominid from the Upper Miocene of Chad, Central Africa.' Nature, 418, 145–151. A subsequently described femur fragment from the same site has been argued by some researchers to show quadrupedal, not bipedal, locomotion, reopening the question of whether Sahelanthropus belongs on the human lineage at all rather than being an early, unrelated ape.

entries.label: Neanderthal Genome Project
entries.loc: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, Leipzig, Germany
entries.hint: A team led by Svante Pääbo sequenced a first draft of the Neanderthal nuclear genome from fossil bone fragments, overcoming severe DNA degradation and contamination challenges. Comparison with living humans revealed that non-African populations carry roughly 1–2% Neanderthal DNA, providing the first direct genetic proof of interbreeding between Neanderthals and the modern humans who left Africa.
entries.note: Green, R.E. et al. (2010). 'A Draft Sequence of the Neanderthal Genome.' Science, 328(5979), 710–722. Pääbo received the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for pioneering ancient-genome sequencing methods. The admixture finding (see ef4) has been repeatedly confirmed and refined with higher-coverage genomes and larger modern reference panels.

entries.label: Denisovan Discovery
entries.loc: Denisova Cave, Altai Mountains, Siberia, Russia
entries.hint: DNA extracted from a single small finger bone fragment revealed an entirely new archaic human population, genetically distinct from both Neanderthals and modern humans, that had never been identified from anatomy alone — the first hominin group in history to be discovered purely through its genome rather than through recognisable skeletal remains.
entries.note: Reich, D. et al. (2010). 'Genetic History of an Archaic Hominin Group from Denisova Cave in Siberia.' Nature, 468, 1053–1060. Denisovan DNA is found at especially high levels (roughly 4–6%) in modern Melanesian and Aboriginal Australian populations, and a Denisovan-derived EPAS1 gene variant confers high-altitude adaptation in Tibetans (see st12) — a rare, well-documented case of adaptive introgression from an extinct human lineage.

entries.label: Mitochondrial Eve Study
entries.hint: Comparing mitochondrial DNA, inherited only through the maternal line, across 147 people from five geographic populations, the study traced all living humans' mitochondrial lineages back to a single common ancestral woman who lived in Africa roughly 200,000 years ago — the first genetic evidence directly supporting a recent, single African origin for modern humans, independent of the fossil record.
entries.note: Cann, R.L., Stoneking, M. & Wilson, A.C. (1987). 'Mitochondrial DNA and Human Evolution.' Nature, 325, 31–36. The original phylogenetic tree-building method was shown to be statistically flawed (Templeton 1992, Science) and did not uniquely support an African root over thousands of other trees of similar length; the core African-origin conclusion has since been robustly confirmed by much larger, methodologically rigorous nuclear genome studies.

entries.label: Gombe Chimpanzee Tool Use
entries.hint: Jane Goodall observed a wild chimpanzee, David Greybeard, strip leaves from a twig and insert it into a termite mound to fish out termites to eat — the first documented case of tool making, not just tool use, by a non-human animal. The finding overturned the long-held assumption that toolmaking was a uniquely human behaviour separating people from the rest of the animal kingdom.
entries.note: Goodall, J. (1964). 'Tool-Using and Aimed Throwing in a Community of Free-Living Chimpanzees.' Nature, 201, 1264–1266. Subsequent decades of field research across multiple chimpanzee populations documented dozens of distinct, socially transmitted tool traditions (see ef8), establishing that behavioural, not just genetic, variation is widespread among wild chimpanzees.

entries.label: Ardipithecus ramidus ("Ardi")
entries.hint: First found in 1994 but not fully described until 2009 due to the extreme fragility of the bones, this 4.4-million-year-old skeleton is far older than Lucy and shows a surprising mix: a grasping, opposable big toe suited for tree climbing, alongside pelvic features suggesting some capacity for upright walking on the ground — evidence that the earliest bipedalism may have evolved in a wooded, not savanna, habitat.
entries.note: White, T.D. et al. (2009). 'Ardipithecus ramidus and the Paleobiology of Early Hominids.' Science, 326(5949), 64–86. The claimed degree of habitual bipedalism remains disputed (Harcourt-Smith 2010, Nature); the wooded palaeoenvironmental context is well established and was central to challenging the savanna hypothesis (see th3).

entries.label: EPAS1 Tibetan Altitude Adaptation
entries.loc: University of California, Berkeley, California / BGI, Shenzhen, China
entries.hint: Genomic scans of Tibetan highlanders identified a variant of the EPAS1 gene, which regulates the body's response to low oxygen, at unusually high frequency — allowing Tibetans to avoid the excessive, harmful overproduction of red blood cells that lowlanders experience at high altitude. The adaptive variant was later shown to have entered the Tibetan gene pool through interbreeding with Denisovans.
entries.note: Yi, X. et al. (2010). 'Sequencing of 50 Human Exomes Reveals Adaptation to High Altitude.' Science, 329(5987), 75–78. The Denisovan origin of the adaptive EPAS1 variant was demonstrated by Huerta-Sánchez, E. et al. (2014). 'Altitude Adaptation in Tibetans Caused by Introgression of Denisovan-like DNA.' Nature, 512, 194–197 — one of the clearest documented cases of adaptive introgression from an archaic human lineage in the modern genome.

entries.label: Olduvai Gorge Potassium-Argon Dating
entries.hint: Applying the newly developed potassium-argon radiometric dating technique to volcanic ash layers at Olduvai Gorge, geochronologists dated the base of Bed I — and the Zinjanthropus (Paranthropus boisei) and early Homo habilis fossils Louis and Mary Leakey had found there — to roughly 1.75 million years old, nearly quadrupling the previously assumed age of the earliest stone-tool-making hominins.
entries.note: Leakey, L.S.B., Evernden, J.F. & Curtis, G.H. (1961). 'Age of Bed I, Olduvai Gorge, Tanganyika.' Nature, 191, 478–479. The result was independently cross-checked against fission-track dating of the same ash layers (Fleischer et al. 1965, Science) and confirmed, establishing potassium-argon dating as a reliable method for East African hominin sites and anchoring the whole subsequent chronology of human origins research.

categories.label: Effects & Phenomena
categories.subtitle: Named, replicable patterns in human biological adaptation and variation

entries.label: Lactase Persistence
entries.hint: Most mammals lose the ability to digest lactose after weaning, but a genetic mutation allowing continued lactase enzyme production into adulthood swept to high frequency (over 90%) in Northern European and some African and Middle Eastern pastoralist populations within the last 7,000-10,000 years — one of the fastest, strongest cases of natural selection ever measured directly in the human genome.
entries.note: Enattah, N.S. et al. (2002). 'Identification of a Variant Associated with Adult-Type Hypolactasia.' Nature Genetics, 30, 233–237, pinpointed the European -13910*T allele. Tishkoff, S.A. et al. (2007, Nature Genetics) found independent, different mutations conferring the same trait in East African pastoralist populations — a striking case of convergent evolution to the same cultural practice, dairying, arising from different genetic routes.

entries.label: Sickle-Cell Trait & Malaria Resistance
entries.hint: A single mutated haemoglobin gene, lethal in its homozygous form (causing sickle-cell disease), is carried at surprisingly high frequency in malaria-endemic regions because carrying just one copy confers substantial resistance to severe malaria — a textbook case of heterozygote advantage, where a genetically 'bad' trait persists in a population because it is beneficial in a specific dose in a specific environment.
entries.note: Allison, A.C. (1954). 'Protection Afforded by Sickle-Cell Trait Against Subtertian Malarial Infection.' British Medical Journal, 1(4857), 290–294, based on fieldwork in Uganda. The resistance mechanism was later shown (Cyrklaff, M. et al. 2011, Science) to work partly by impairing the malaria parasite's ability to export proteins to the surface of infected red blood cells, refining the original correlational finding into a demonstrated causal mechanism.

entries.label: Skin Pigmentation Gradient
entries.loc: California Academy of Sciences, San Francisco, California
entries.hint: Human skin colour varies gradually with latitude, correlating closely with the intensity of ultraviolet radiation: darker skin evolved near the equator to protect against UV-induced folate degradation and skin cancer, while lighter skin evolved at higher latitudes to allow enough UV penetration for the body to synthesise adequate vitamin D — a balance between two opposing selective pressures rather than one-directional selection.
entries.note: Jablonski, N.G. & Chaplin, G. (2000). 'The Evolution of Human Skin Coloration.' Journal of Human Evolution, 39(1), 57–106. Genetic work (Crawford, N.G. et al. 2017, Science) later showed that even within Africa, skin-colour genetic variation is far more complex than a simple light/dark gradient, with several independently evolved lightening and darkening alleles shared across otherwise distantly related populations.

entries.label: Neanderthal Admixture in Non-African Genomes
entries.hint: Every present-day human population outside Africa carries measurable Neanderthal ancestry, typically 1–2% of the genome, concentrated in genes related to skin, hair, and immune function while conspicuously absent from genes related to male fertility and certain brain regions — a pattern suggesting some hybrid offspring were less biologically fit, a phenomenon called selection against introgression.
entries.note: Sankararaman, S. et al. (2014). 'The Genomic Landscape of Neanderthal Ancestry in Present-Day Humans.' Nature, 507, 354–357. East Asian populations were later found to carry slightly higher Neanderthal ancestry than European populations (Wall, J.D. et al. 2013; Vernot, B. & Akey, J.M. 2015), a difference still not fully explained, possibly reflecting a second, distinct interbreeding pulse.

entries.label: Encephalization Trend in Homo
entries.hint: Average cranial capacity within the genus Homo roughly tripled over about 2 million years, from around 600 cubic centimetres in early Homo habilis to roughly 1,350 cubic centimetres in modern Homo sapiens — but the rate of increase was not steady, showing distinct accelerations rather than one smooth, continuous climb.
entries.note: McHenry, H.M. (1994). 'Tempo and Mode in Human Evolution.' Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 91(15), 6780–6786, quantified the trend across the hominin fossil record. Brain size increase does not track tightly with behavioural sophistication at every step — Homo naledi (see st5) had a brain barely a third the size of a modern human's despite behaviourally complex, disputed cave use, and Homo floresiensis retained a small brain long after larger-brained Homo species existed elsewhere.

entries.label: Postcranial Robusticity Decline
entries.hint: Human skeletons have become progressively less robust — thinner bone cortices, smaller joint surfaces, lighter overall build — over the last 30,000 to 10,000 years, most sharply coinciding with the shift from a highly physically demanding foraging lifestyle to sedentary farming, indicating that mechanical loading during life, not just genetics, substantially shapes adult skeletal robustness.
entries.note: Ruff, C.B., Trinkaus, E. & Holliday, T.W. (1993). 'Postcranial Robusticity in Homo I: Temporal Trends and Mechanical Interpretation.' American Journal of Physical Anthropology, 91(1), 21–53. Because bone responds plastically to mechanical loading during an individual's life (Wolff's Law), the gracilization trend reflects a mix of genuine genetic change and lifestyle-driven developmental plasticity, and disentangling the two contributions remains methodologically difficult.

entries.label: The Obstetric Dilemma
entries.hint: Because a narrow, bipedal-adapted pelvis limits how wide the birth canal can be, while a large fetal brain requires a wide head to pass through it, human babies are born at an earlier, more neurologically immature developmental stage relative to other primates, and human childbirth is unusually difficult compared to other apes' — a proposed evolutionary trade-off between two conflicting selective pressures.
entries.note: Washburn, S.L. (1960). 'Tools and Human Evolution.' Scientific American, 203(3), 62–75, first framed the pelvis-brain trade-off. The 'dilemma' framing has been challenged (Dunsworth, H.M. et al. 2012, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) by the competing 'energetics of gestation and growth' model, which argues maternal metabolic limits, not pelvic width alone, better explain the timing of human birth — the strict obstetric-dilemma version is now considered only a partial explanation.

entries.label: Chimpanzee Cultural Variation
entries.loc: University of St Andrews, St Andrews, Scotland
entries.hint: Different wild chimpanzee communities across Africa use different, socially learned tool techniques and behaviours — some crack nuts with stone hammers, others fish for termites with different tool designs, others use leaves as napkins — variation that cannot be explained by genetics or local ecology alone, meeting the criteria researchers use to define 'culture' in animals.
entries.note: Whiten, A. et al. (1999). 'Cultures in Chimpanzees.' Nature, 399, 682–685, synthesising decades of field data across seven long-term study sites. Some later critics (Boesch, C. 2003) argued particular behavioural differences could still partly reflect subtle undetected ecological variation rather than pure social transmission, though the cumulative case across dozens of behaviours is now widely accepted as genuine cultural variation.

entries.label: Dental Reduction Trend in Homo
entries.hint: Tooth size, particularly molars, has shrunk substantially across the genus Homo over the last two million years, and the trend accelerated sharply after the invention of cooking and food processing technology, roughly tracking a reduced need for heavy chewing to break down raw, fibrous food.
entries.note: Calcagno, J.M. & Gibson, K.R. (1988). 'Human Dental Reduction: Natural Selection or the Probable Mutation Effect.' American Journal of Physical Anthropology, 77(4), 505–517. Whether the reduction is primarily adaptive (driven by softer cooked diets reducing the need for large chewing surfaces) or a largely neutral, non-adaptive genetic drift effect remains an open, actively contested question in the dental anthropology literature.

categories.label: Key Concepts
categories.subtitle: The building blocks and vocabulary every student must command

entries.label: Bipedalism
entries.hint: Walking habitually upright on two legs, rather than knuckle-walking or brachiating like other apes, is the single most defining anatomical trait separating hominins from all other primates — it preceded large brain size, tool use, and language by millions of years and reshaped nearly every part of the skeleton from the skull's attachment point to the feet.
entries.note: Darwin, C. (1871). The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex. John Murray, first proposed that upright walking, tool use, and reduced canine teeth evolved together as an interconnected package — a claim since substantially revised, since fossil evidence (see st2, st11) shows bipedalism evolved millions of years before stone tools or significant brain expansion.

entries.label: Encephalization Quotient
entries.loc: University of California, Los Angeles, California
entries.hint: Because larger animals simply need larger brains to run a larger body, raw brain size alone is a poor measure of relative brain enlargement across species — the encephalization quotient instead compares a species' actual brain size to the brain size predicted for a typical mammal of its body mass, giving a standardised way to compare 'braininess' across very differently sized animals.
entries.note: Jerison, H.J. (1973). Evolution of the Brain and Intelligence. Academic Press, established the standard formula. Humans have an EQ of roughly 7 — about seven times what would be predicted for a typical mammal of our body size — the highest of any living species, though the metric has been criticised (Deaner, R.O. et al. 2007, Brain, Behavior and Evolution) for not accounting for how brain tissue is actually distributed across different functional regions.

entries.label: Morphospecies Concept in Paleoanthropology
entries.loc: American Museum of Natural History, New York, New York
entries.hint: Because fossil species cannot be tested for interbreeding the way living species can, paleoanthropologists must classify extinct hominins into species based on physical similarity alone — a method that is inherently more subjective than the biological species concept and is the direct root cause of the field's frequent, sometimes bitter, disagreements over how many hominin species actually existed.
entries.note: Mayr, E. (1950). 'Taxonomic Categories in Fossil Hominids.' Cold Spring Harbor Symposia on Quantitative Biology, 15, 109–118, argued forcefully for taxonomic lumping of early hominin fossils into few species. The tension Mayr identified directly underlies the ongoing lumper-versus-splitter debate (see db2) that still divides the field today.

entries.label: Sexual Dimorphism
entries.hint: The degree of body-size or canine-size difference between males and females of a species correlates, across living primates, with mating system and the intensity of male-male competition — highly dimorphic species tend toward polygyny, while lightly dimorphic species tend toward more monogamous pair-bonding, giving paleoanthropologists an indirect tool for inferring extinct hominins' likely social structure from fossil bones alone.
entries.note: Plavcan, J.M. & van Schaik, C.P. (1997). 'Interpreting Hominid Behavior on the Basis of Sexual Dimorphism.' Journal of Human Evolution, 32(4), 345–374. Early Australopithecus shows relatively high body-size dimorphism, more like a modern gorilla than a modern human, suggesting a more polygynous social structure than Lovejoy's monogamy-driven provisioning model (see th5) would predict — a significant point of tension between the fossil dimorphism evidence and that theory.

entries.label: Life History Theory
entries.loc: University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, New Mexico
entries.hint: Life history theory analyses how organisms allocate limited energy between competing priorities — growth, reproduction, and survival — across their lifespan; applied to human evolution, it explains humans' unusually slow, extended childhood, late age of first reproduction, and long post-reproductive lifespan as a coordinated package tied to reliance on complex, learned skills for foraging.
entries.note: Kaplan, H., Hill, K., Lancaster, J. & Hurtado, A.M. (2000). 'A Theory of Human Life History Evolution: Diet, Intelligence, and Longevity.' Evolutionary Anthropology, 9(4), 156–185, drawing on decades of fieldwork among the Ache and Hiwi foraging peoples of South America. The framework directly incorporates the grandmother hypothesis (see th7) as one part of the broader life-history package rather than a standalone explanation.

entries.label: Founder Effect & Genetic Drift
entries.loc: American Museum of Natural History, New York, New York
entries.hint: When a small group splinters off from a larger population to found a new one — as happened repeatedly as modern humans dispersed out of Africa and across the globe — the new population carries only a random, reduced sample of the parent population's genetic variation, which is why genetic diversity decreases in a smooth gradient the further a population's ancestors travelled from East Africa.
entries.note: Mayr, E. (1942). Systematics and the Origin of Species. Columbia University Press, coined the term 'founder effect' within general evolutionary theory. The 'serial founder effect' model of human dispersal was quantitatively confirmed by genome-wide data (Ramachandran, S. et al. 2005, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences), which found genetic diversity decreases in a striking straight-line relationship with geographic distance from Ethiopia.

entries.label: Taphonomy
entries.hint: Taphonomy is the study of everything that happens to an organism's remains between death and discovery as a fossil — scavenging, weathering, water transport, burial, and mineral replacement — all of which can distort or destroy evidence, so interpreting any fossil find requires first reconstructing its taphonomic history to know how much the assemblage has been altered from the original living population it represents.
entries.note: Efremov, I.A. (1940). 'Taphonomy: A New Branch of Paleontology.' Pan-American Geologist, 74, 81–93, coined the term from the Greek for 'burial laws.' Taphonomic analysis was central to resolving the Homo naledi deliberate-disposal debate (see db8, st5), since alternative, non-behavioural explanations had to be ruled out via careful study of the bone assemblage before the disposal hypothesis could even be considered.

entries.label: Clinal Variation
entries.loc: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan
entries.hint: Human biological traits like skin colour, body shape, and many genetic markers vary gradually and continuously across geography, tracking environmental gradients like latitude or altitude, rather than clustering into the sharply bounded, discrete categories that the folk concept of 'race' assumes — a single trait's cline rarely lines up neatly with another trait's cline, undermining any attempt to sort humanity into a small number of natural, biologically coherent groups.
entries.note: Livingstone, F.B. (1962). 'On the Non-Existence of Human Races.' Current Anthropology, 3(3), 279–281. Genome-wide studies (Rosenberg, N.A. et al. 2002, Science) later showed that while genetic clustering algorithms can be made to produce groupings that loosely track continental geography when forced to a small number of clusters, the vast majority of total human genetic variation (roughly 85–90%) exists within, not between, those clusters — directly informing the modern race debate (see db5).
